entries.a: Hey {name}! Great to see you. What can I help with today - jobs near you, applications, or your profile?
f: How do I find jobs near me?

entries.a: I'm doing great, thanks for asking! I'm ready to help you land your next freelance gig. What do you need?
I'm Bridgey, SkillBridge's in-app assistant. I answer questions about using the app and freelancing as a student. I'm a simple built-in helper, so I work best with clear, specific questions.

I can help with: finding nearby jobs on the map, searching and filtering projects, writing applications, understanding your application status, messaging clients, improving your profile, pricing your work, staying safe from scams, and general freelancing tips. Just ask!
You're welcome! Anything else I can help you with?
Bye {name}! Good luck out there - I'll be here whenever you need me.
Why did the freelancer bring a ladder to the meeting? They heard the client wanted to take things to the next level. 😄
Every freelancer you admire started with zero reviews and a rough first proposal. Keep applying, keep improving each pitch, and celebrate small wins - a shortlist is progress. You've got this!

SkillBridge connects college students with freelance opportunities posted by clients. You build a profile, browse or search projects, apply with an intro and resume link, track your application through the pipeline, and chat with the client once you're shortlisted or accepted.
SkillBridge is free for students to join, browse and apply. Payment terms for a project are agreed between you and the client.
Tap 'Create account' on the login screen, choose whether you're a Student or a Client, enter your name, email and password, then complete your profile. It takes about two minutes.

Double-check your email and password (passwords are case-sensitive). If you can't remember it, use 'Forgot password' on the login screen to get a reset email. Also make sure you have an internet connection.
On the login screen tap 'Forgot password', enter your email, and we'll send a reset link. Check your spam folder if it doesn't arrive in a few minutes.
Open the Profile tab and tap 'Log out' at the bottom of the screen.
Account deletion isn't available inside the app yet. If you need your data removed, contact the SkillBridge team and we'll take care of it.
Your sign-in email is tied to your account and can't be changed from the app right now. You can create a new account with the new address if needed.
Go to the Profile tab and tap 'Edit profile'. Fill in your degree, college, graduation year, skills, experience, a short bio and your resume link. A complete profile gets noticed far more by clients.

Tips for a strong profile: 1) add 5-8 real skills, 2) write a 2-3 line bio about what you can deliver, 3) add a resume or portfolio link, 4) set your location so you appear in nearby searches, and 5) mention any projects, internships or coursework. Profiles with skills and a bio also get better AI match scores.

A good bio is short and outcome-focused: 'Third-year CS student who builds clean Android apps in Kotlin. Delivered 3 college projects and an internship app. Available 15 hrs/week.' Say what you do, one proof point, and your availability.

List skills you can actually deliver. In-demand ones on freelance boards: web development (React, HTML/CSS), Android/Flutter, Python, data analysis (Excel, SQL), UI/UX (Figma), graphic design (Canva, Photoshop), content writing, SEO, social media and video editing. Matching your skills to project requirements raises your match score.

SkillBridge uses a resume *link* rather than a file upload. Upload your resume to Google Drive (or similar), set sharing to 'Anyone with the link can view', and paste that link in your profile and when applying.

Keep your resume to one page: contact info, 2-line summary, skills, projects (with a link and what you built), education, and any internships. Lead with projects if you have little experience, use action verbs, and add numbers where possible (e.g. 'reduced load time by 40%').
Your profile shows an avatar with your initials by default. A clear, friendly photo link in your profile helps build trust with clients.
Open the Explore tab to browse every open project. You can search by title, skill or company, filter by category, budget and distance, and sort by newest or 'Recommended For You'.
Use the search bar at the top of Explore - it matches project titles, company names and required skills. Try searching a skill like 'Figma' or 'Python'.
In Explore you can filter by category (Development, Design, Writing, Marketing, Data, Other), budget band, and distance, and sort by newest or by how well a project matches you.
Projects fall into six categories: Development, Design, Writing, Marketing, Data, and Other. Use the category chips in Explore to focus on the one that fits you.

Open the Nearby Jobs screen: it shows an OpenStreetMap with red pins for projects around you, a blue dot for your location, and a list sorted by distance. Pick a radius (5-100 km) or choose a city if your GPS isn't available.
f: Why can't I see my location?

entries.a: The map is powered by OpenStreetMap. Red pins are projects, the blue dot is you. Tap a pin to see the project and open its details. You can pinch to zoom and drag to explore. Remote projects don't have a pin because they can be done from anywhere.

Allow location when the app asks, and make sure GPS/Location is switched on in your phone settings. On an emulator, set a location in the extended controls. If it still doesn't work, pick your city from the chips on the Nearby screen instead.
Your exact GPS position is only used on your device to calculate distances. When your location is shown to others it is rounded to roughly a 1 km area so your precise position stays private.
Pick a radius (5, 10, 25, 50 or 100 km) on the Nearby screen or the distance chips in Explore. Distances are straight-line from your current location to the project's location.
Many projects are Remote, meaning you can do them from anywhere. Look for 'Remote' on the project card. Remote projects don't show on the map since they have no fixed location.
Hybrid projects mix remote work with occasional on-site days at the client's city. They appear on the map at that city so you can judge the commute.
'Recommended For You' ranks projects by how well they fit your skills, interests and location - shown as a match percentage with reasons. Open the AI Match Assistant to see your top matches.
Open a project, tap 'Apply', write a short intro explaining why you're a good fit, paste your resume link, and submit. You'll see a confirmation and can track it under the Applications tab.

A winning intro is 4-6 lines: 1) greet the client and name the project, 2) say exactly how you'll solve their problem, 3) share one relevant project or skill, 4) mention your availability and timeline, 5) close politely. Avoid copy-paste messages - clients can tell.

Try: 'Hi! I'm {name}, a student with hands-on experience in [skill]. I've built [relevant project] and can deliver your [project] in [X days]. I'm available [hours/week] and happy to share samples. My resume is linked below. Thanks for your time!'
You can apply to each project only once - the app prevents duplicates. If you already applied, track it in the Applications tab. You can message the client once you're shortlisted or accepted.
Withdrawing isn't supported in the app yet. If you've changed your mind, message the client (once messaging is unlocked) and let them know politely.

q: how many projects should i apply
entries.a: There's no strict limit. Quality beats quantity though - aim for a few well-tailored applications a day rather than dozens of generic ones.
Applications move through: Applied -> Under Review -> Shortlisted -> Accepted. Or Applied -> Rejected. Open the Applications tab to see where each one stands in the pipeline.
'Applied' means your application is submitted and waiting for the client to open it. Nothing more to do right now - sit tight!
'Under Review' means the client has opened your application and is evaluating candidates. It's a good sign - you're being considered.
Congrats! 'Shortlisted' means you're among the client's top candidates. Messaging unlocks at this stage, so reply quickly and professionally.
Amazing - you got the project! Message the client to confirm scope, timeline, deliverables and payment terms before you start.
Rejections are normal in freelancing, even for experienced pros. Tailor your next intro, strengthen your profile, and keep applying. Each application sharpens your pitch.
Response times vary - some clients reply within a day, others take a week. If you're still 'Applied' after several days, keep applying to other projects. Don't wait on one opportunity.
Messaging unlocks when your application reaches Shortlisted or Accepted. Then open the Messages tab to chat with the client.
To prevent spam, chat only opens once a client shortlists or accepts your application. Until then, make your application and profile as strong as you can.
Be prompt, polite and specific. Confirm scope and deadlines in writing, ask clarifying questions early, share progress updates, and never promise what you can't deliver.
Tap the bell icon on the Home screen to see updates like status changes and new messages. Unread ones are highlighted.

SkillBridge helps you find and win work; payment terms are agreed directly with the client. Confirm the amount, milestones and payment method in chat before you start, and keep records of what was agreed.

As a student, start by estimating hours x a fair hourly rate (₹200-600/hr is common for beginners, more for specialised skills), then compare with the project's listed budget. Quote fixed prices for clear tasks and add a buffer for revisions.
If the budget is low, politely propose a reduced scope or a higher fee for extras. Explain the value you bring. Never undercut yourself so much you resent the work.
The budget on a project card is the total the client plans to pay for the whole project. Use the budget filter in Explore (Under 10k, 10k-20k, Over 20k) to narrow things down.

Start with small, clearly-scoped projects (₹2-10k) in a skill you're confident in. Deliver early, communicate often, and ask for feedback. Your first few successful projects become your portfolio. Build credibility before aiming high.

No experience? Show projects instead: college assignments, personal apps, mock designs, open-source contributions, or volunteer work for a club. Put links in your resume and intro. Clients care about proof you can deliver.

Build a simple portfolio: 3-5 best projects with a screenshot, a one-line problem/solution, tools used, and a live or GitHub link. Use GitHub for code, Behance/Dribbble for design, Medium or a Google Doc for writing samples.
Block fixed freelance hours around classes, be honest about your availability in your intro, pad deadlines by 20%, and avoid taking work during exam weeks. Communicate early if something slips.
If you might miss a deadline, tell the client as early as possible with a revised date and what you'll deliver first. Clients forgive delays far more easily than silence.
Agree on scope and a set number of revisions up front. When a request goes beyond that, politely say it's outside the original scope and offer a quote for the extra work.

Stay safe: keep chats inside the app, never pay money to get a job, avoid clients who push you off-platform immediately, be wary of unrealistic pay, and never share bank/OTP details. Agree on milestones so you're paid for completed work. Report anything suspicious to the SkillBridge team.

q: how to spot a bad client
entries.a: Red flags: vague scope, pressure to start free 'trial' work, refusing to discuss payment, unrealistic deadlines, asking for personal/bank details, or being rude in the first messages. Trust your gut and walk away if it feels off.
Be careful with unpaid trials. A tiny paid test or showing your existing portfolio is fair; delivering a full free project is not. You should be paid for your time.
Even for small projects, write down the scope, deliverables, deadline, price and payment schedule in the chat (or a short doc). For bigger jobs, send a simple invoice when you deliver.

Freelance income is generally taxable. As a student with modest earnings you may fall under the basic exemption limit, but rules vary - check with a tax professional or the official income tax portal for your situation.

Web projects are popular. To stand out: show 2-3 deployed sites (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel), write clean responsive layouts, and mention frameworks (React, Node) in your skills. Search 'React' or 'Website' in Explore.

Mobile dev gigs pay well. Showcase an app on GitHub or a demo APK/video, mention Kotlin/Flutter/React Native, and highlight things like Firebase, REST APIs, and clean UI. Filter Explore by Development to find them.
Python is great for automation, scraping, backend APIs and data tasks. Show scripts or small tools on GitHub with a clear README. Search 'Python' in Explore to see matching projects.
For UI/UX gigs, share Figma links or case studies that explain the problem, your process, and the final design. Even redesigns of existing apps count. Check the Design category in Explore.
Graphic design clients love variety: logos, posters, social posts and thumbnails. Put your best 6-10 pieces on Behance or a Drive folder and link it in your profile.

For writing gigs, share 2-3 samples (blog posts, articles, product copy), keep grammar spotless, and mention your niche. Meet word counts and deadlines, and clients will come back. See the Writing category.

Marketing clients want results. Show any growth you've driven (followers, clicks, campaigns for college fests) and mention tools like Meta Ads, Google Analytics, Canva, and SEO basics. Browse the Marketing category.

Data gigs range from Excel cleanup to dashboards and ML. Share notebooks or dashboards with a clear question, method and result. SQL, Excel, Python and Power BI/Tableau are high-value skills. See the Data category.
Video editors: put a short showreel (1-2 min) in your portfolio and mention your tools (Premiere, DaVinci, CapCut, After Effects). Fast turnaround on reels and shorts is a big plus.
Language skills are valuable - mention every language you're fluent in plus any specialisation (technical, legal, subtitles). Accuracy and consistent turnaround matter more than speed.
If you can teach, look in the 'Other' category and mention your subjects and grades. Share a sample lesson or past results to build trust with parents and clients.
Before a call: re-read the project, prepare 2-3 questions about scope and goals, have your portfolio ready, and test your audio. Be on time, listen first, and confirm next steps at the end.
A tidy LinkedIn helps: professional photo, a headline with your skill, 2-3 projects, and recommendations from professors or past clients. Share it alongside your resume link.
Pick one in-demand skill and build 2-3 small projects with it - projects beat certificates. Free resources: freeCodeCamp, YouTube tutorials, NPTEL, Coursera audits, Google/Microsoft learning paths.
Reviews aren't in the app yet, but you can ask satisfied clients for a short testimonial and add it to your portfolio or LinkedIn. Always request feedback after delivery.
SkillBridge currently uses a clean light theme. Dark mode may come in a future update.
The app is currently available in English only. More languages may be added later.

Sorry about that! Try: 1) check your internet, 2) close and reopen the app, 3) log out and back in, 4) update to the latest version. If it keeps happening, contact the SkillBridge team with what you were doing.
SkillBridge needs an internet connection for live projects, messages and map tiles. Some data is cached locally, but reconnect to get fresh updates.
For anything I can't solve, reach the SkillBridge team through the support contact in your project handover or the official channel. I'm a built-in helper, so I can't escalate tickets myself.
Clients can see your profile (name, college, skills, bio, resume link) when you apply or when they discover students. Your password is never visible to anyone, and your exact location is generalised.
There's no formal verification step yet. Fill in your college, degree and graduation year honestly - an accurate profile builds trust.
SkillBridge was built as a student-freelance marketplace project. Ask the team for credits and details.
Home shows your progress (applied, in review, shortlisted counts), your latest applications, recommended projects, and the notification bell.

The bottom bar has five tabs: Home (overview), Explore (browse and filter projects), Applications (track your status), Messages (chat with clients) and Profile (your details). Use Nearby Jobs for the map view.
Open the Applications tab to see every project you applied to with its current status. Tap one for the full pipeline and a Message button when chat is unlocked.
Each project lists a deadline on its details page. Apply well before it - clients often review the first applicants first.
Each project lists required skills and experience. If you meet most of them, apply - explain how your projects make up for any gap. Match percentage in 'Recommended For You' helps you judge fit.
Lead with 1-2 core skills you can prove, then list supporting ones. Specialising makes your pitch sharper and your profile easier for clients to trust.
Each application is individual. If a project is large, mention in your intro that you can bring in a teammate - but be clear who is responsible for what.
AI tools can speed up drafts, but always review and personalise the output, and be transparent if a client asks. Your judgement and quality are what clients pay for.
Freelancing fits student life well: pick small, flexible projects, state your weekly hours, and build up gradually. Filter Explore by budget to find quick gigs.
SkillBridge focuses on freelance projects, but they make great resume material for internships and placements. Mention client projects, links and outcomes in your applications.
Matches depend on your profile. Add your skills, interests and location in Edit profile, and the AI Match Assistant will have more to work with.
If the map is empty, try a bigger radius or pick a different city on the Nearby screen. Remote projects aren't pinned because they have no location, so check Explore for those.

On the Nearby screen use the city chips (Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Delhi and more) to centre the map on that city and see projects around it - handy when you're planning to relocate or GPS is off.
Open the Post tab, fill in the title, category, budget, skills, description, responsibilities, requirements, deadline and (optionally) location, then publish. Clear details attract better applicants.

Great listings state the outcome you want, list 3-5 concrete deliverables, mention required skills and the deadline, and give a realistic budget. Specific posts get stronger, more relevant applications.

q: how do i set a budget
entries.a: Estimate the hours the work needs and multiply by a fair hourly rate (₹250-700/hr is typical for students depending on skill). Underpaying attracts low-effort work - a fair budget gets quality.
Use the Discover tab to browse student profiles, search by skill, and see students around you on the map. Open a profile to see skills, college and resume link.
Open one of your projects from the Projects tab and tap 'View proposals' to see everyone who applied. Open a proposal to read the intro, check the profile and update the status.

Look for relevance over polish: do their skills and past projects match your needs, is the intro specific to your project, and do they communicate clearly? Shortlist 2-3, chat with them, and ask a small clarifying question to gauge responsiveness.
Open a proposal and set its status: Under Review, Shortlisted, Accepted or Rejected. Students are notified of each change, and chat unlocks at Shortlisted/Accepted.
Once you shortlist or accept a student, open their proposal and tap 'Message'. Be clear about scope, deadline and budget in your first message.
Clients complete a one-time payment setup after profile setup. Pay students as agreed in chat - split larger projects into milestones so both sides stay protected.
Find your posts in the Projects tab. Open a project to review its proposals and details. For changes to a published project, keep descriptions accurate so students apply with the right expectations.
Be clear about deliverables, set milestones, give timely feedback, and respect that students juggle classes. Fair pay and clear communication earn you your best work.
Warning signs: generic copy-pasted intros, empty profiles, no resume link, or unrealistic promises. Shortlist applicants who reference your project specifically.
Open the AI Match Assistant, pick one of your projects, and it ranks students by how well their skills, interests and location fit - with reasons for each match.
